note: The plesiomorphic locomotor engine of the vertebrate body (Schilling 2011). Two divisions separated by the horizontal septum and marked by the split of the spinal nerve: epaxial above, on dorsal rami; hypaxial below, on ventral rami. That nerve boundary is the same kind of evidence that anchors the dorsal/ventral limb masses, and it is why axial muscles belong in this dataset rather than beside it — the appendicular system is built on top of the axial one and takes over from it.

muscles.name: Epaxial musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic (primaxial); myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum. Innervated by the DORSAL rami of the spinal nerves — the defining criterion.

consensus.origin: Neural spines, transverse processes, zygapophyses and the vertebral centra; in fishes, the myosepta.
consensus.insertion: Successive vertebrae, ribs and the skull; the tracts span many segments in amniotes.
consensus.action: Plesiomorphically mobilisation — lateral bending for swimming. In tetrapods it additionally stabilises the trunk against inertial and limb-muscle forces; in mammals it also serves sagittal mobility and stabilises against the inertia of the body's centre of mass.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Myomeric axial musculature
occurrences.note: Myxine glutinosa, the animal in Schilling's Fig. 2 — a hagfish, not a lamprey. This row previously claimed a lamprey, which Schilling does not examine. Segmental myomeres separated by myosepta, undivided into tracts, with dorsal and ventral myomere parts innervated by separate rami of the ventral root: axial-based locomotion in its plesiomorphic form.

occurrences.name: Epaxial myomeres
occurrences.note: Etmopterus spinax, the velvet belly lantern shark sectioned behind the anus in Schilling's Fig. 2 (Sudan black B, after Kryvi). Divided from the hypaxial by the horizontal septum but still strictly segmental. The row previously claimed a holocephalan, which Schilling does not examine.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis trunci
occurrences.note: Ambystoma tigrinum, whose 4th external trunk segment is the salamander section in Schilling's Fig. 2. The dorsalis trunci retains much of the segmental fish arrangement, and lateral undulation still contributes to locomotion alongside the limbs. Fetcho & Reich (1992) is the source for its motor pools, which are NOT segregated into epaxial and hypaxial pools despite terrestrial locomotion.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis trunci
occurrences.note: Greatly shortened with the reduced presacral column and the urostyle.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Discoglossus pictus, Prikryl et al. (2009), from the review table and the baseline description. Longissimus dorsi, from the sacral and presacral vertebrae onto the urostyle, rotating it dorsally. In anurans the epaxial series has been rebuilt around a rigid trunk and a rod: it moves one bone rather than bending a column.

Discoglossus and Ascaphus, from Prikryl et al.'s review table and descriptions. Longissimus dorsi, from the sacral and presacral vertebrae onto the urostyle, rotating it dorsally. In anurans the epaxial series has been rebuilt around a rigid trunk and a rod: it moves one bone rather than bending a column.

Discoglossus pictus, Prikryl et al. (2009). From the dorsal side of the sacral diapophysis to the dorsolateral surface of the posterior two-thirds of the urostyle, partly covered by the longissimus dorsi. Filed with the longissimus dorsi on this record: Prikryl et al.'s own table groups the two as the axial-to-axial muscles, and both run the presacral or sacral series onto the rod. Function is given as lateral bending at the iliosacral joint when one side acts and trunk stiffening with moderate dorsal rotation of the urostyle when both do — which is the anuran epaxial series doing a job no other tetrapod's does. `sacral-vertebrae` carries the diapophysis, since the skeleton has no separate element for it.

occurrences.name: Transversospinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis
occurrences.note: Reorganised into three longitudinal, polysegmental tracts — the amniote condition. Cieri (2018) documents the regionalisation along the varanid column.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus. Left unscored on the source's own instruction: Cieri (2018) writes that the anatomy of the epaxial muscles — longissimus dorsi, transversospinalis and iliocostalis — 'including details of insertion and origin tendons, have been described in detail previously (Gasc, 1981; Ritter, 1995; Tsuihiji, 2007) and will not be described here.' **This is a pointer, not a gap**: those three papers are what would close the lepidosaur epaxial column, and none of them is in the corpus. Cieri's contribution to the epaxial series is the supracostalis dorsus brevis, which is scored.

occurrences.name: Transversospinal system, longissimus, iliocostalis
occurrences.action: Stabilises the trunk against sagittal components of limb-muscle action; permits and controls the sagittal bending of the mammalian back.
occurrences.note: Microtus arvalis, the common vole sectioned between the 6th and 7th lumbar vertebrae in Schilling's Fig. 2 — his mammal for perivertebral fibre types, and so the animal behind the claim that the transversospinal muscle subdivides into the transversospinal system (multifidus, semispinalis and relatives). Schilling ties that subdivision to the evolution of a mobile lumbar region and a rib-free lumbar segment.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Microtus arvalis. Origin: Neural spines, transverse processes and the sacrum. Insertion: Successive vertebrae, ribs and the occiput. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment.

occurrences.name: Erector spinae and the transversospinal system
occurrences.action: Extends and laterally bends the trunk and neck; the suboccipital group extends and rotates the head on the atlas and axis.
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of the spinal nerves, segmentally from C1 to S5.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **One field, segmentally supplied from the top of the neck to the sacrum, and every human name in it is a regional label rather than a muscle.** Gest lists erector spinae, iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis, semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores, interspinales, intertransversarii, splenius and the four suboccipital muscles, and gives all of them dorsal primary rami. That single fact is what makes the field one homology group: an epaxial muscle is defined by its nerve, not by its attachments, and this is the column where the definition is easiest to check. The three named tracts have their own records and are scored there.

**Splenius capitis** (Gest). Nuchal ligament and the spines of the last cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae, forward and upward to the mastoid process and the lateral end of the superior nuchal line. Its fibre direction is why it is worth separating: it runs spine-to-skull, obliquely across the transversospinal sheet beneath it, which runs transverse-process-to-spine. Two layers of one segmental series crossing each other, both on dorsal rami. Gest lists an undivided splenius as well as the capitis and cervicis parts, so the three entries are two insertions of one muscle.

**Splenius cervicis** (Gest). Same origin as the capitis part, ending instead on the posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of the first three cervical vertebrae.

**Obliquus capitis inferior** (Gest). Spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas — the one suboccipital muscle that never reaches the skull. It rotates the atlas, and the head rides on it.

**Obliquus capitis superior** (Gest). Transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone above the inferior nuchal line.

**Rectus capitis posterior major** (Gest). Spine of the axis to the inferior nuchal line. With the two obliqui it bounds the suboccipital triangle, and all four suboccipital muscles take the dorsal ramus of C1. That is the whole reason the group is epaxial: nothing about where they attach separates them from the prevertebral muscles a centimetre away, and the nerve does.

**Rectus capitis posterior minor** (Gest). Posterior tubercle of the atlas to the medial part of the inferior nuchal line, deep and medial to the major. The atlas has no spine, which is why the two recti capitis posteriores start on different kinds of thing.

occurrences.name: Longissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ascaphus truei, Prikryl et al. (2009). Inserts along the whole dorsolateral surface of the urostyle **except the tip, which remains uncovered** — the difference from *Discoglossus*, where it runs the full length. Anterior to the sacral vertebra it cannot be told apart from the iliolumbaris except that the iliolumbaris ends on the anterior margin of the sacral diapophysis while this muscle continues onto the urostyle.

occurrences.name: Longissimus dorsi–coccygeosacralis complex
occurrences.attachmentNote: Barbourula busuangensis, Prikryl et al. (2009). Inserts along the whole length of the urostyle. **The coccygeosacralis is not differentiated from the longissimus dorsi here** — behind the sacral diapophysis the two run as one muscle mass laterally, leaving only the cartilaginous rim of the diapophysis uncovered. That lateral portion is itself in two layers, one attached to the sacral diapophysis dorsally and a noticeably thinner one ventrally, which is why the row carries the diapophysis on both sides. In front of the diapophysis the lateral part of the complex is confluent with the iliolumbaris — but the iliolumbaris proper is separate from the longissimus dorsi, unlike in *Ascaphus* where the two cannot be told apart.

occurrences.name: Coccygeosacralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Bufo guttatus, Prikryl et al. (2009). Origin on the **posterior edge** of the sacral diapophysis — a narrower attachment than *Discoglossus*, which takes its dorsal side, and than *Pelobates*, which runs the whole urostyle beneath the longissimus.

occurrences.name: Dorsalis trunci
occurrences.attachmentNote: Caudata (generalised), Prikryl et al. (2009). The trunk musculature of every caudate, neotenic or metamorphosed, consists of myomeres separated by myosepta, as in fish; the dorsal portions of those myomeres form the longitudinal bundle of the dorsalis trunci. Its deeper layers attach to the neural arches of the vertebrae, its fibres running between successive myosepta in an approximately anteroposterior direction. **This is the arrangement the anuran epaxial series is a departure from** — Prikryl et al. use it as the outgroup condition against which the frogs' shortened, urostyle-driven system is read.

occurrences.name: Coccygeosacralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pelobates fuscus, Prikryl et al. (2009). Runs along the **whole length** of the urostyle, below the attachment of the longissimus dorsi, and attaches to the dorsal surface of the sacral diapophysis. *Discoglossus* has it from the diapophysis to the posterior two-thirds of the urostyle; in *Ascaphus* it cannot be separated from the coccygeoiliacus, in *Barbourula* not from the longissimus, and in *Xenopus* and *Pipa* it is absent.

occurrences.name: Longissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pipa pipa, Prikryl et al. (2009). A broad muscle covering the dorsum and part of the flanks, attached posteriorly to the urostyle and to the fascia of the coccygeoiliacus — the fascial end carried as `muscle: iliocaudalis`. **The coccygeosacralis is absent**, as in *Xenopus*.

occurrences.name: Longissimus dorsi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis, Prikryl et al. (2009). Lies in a deeper layer than usual, beneath the latissimus dorsi, attached as in *Discoglossus* to the transverse processes of the vertebrae, and inserting posteriorly on the lateral surface of the **anterior two-thirds** of the urostyle. Compare *Ascaphus*, where it runs the whole dorsolateral length except the tip, and *Discoglossus*, where it takes the whole length.
occurrences.note: **The coccygeosacralis is absent in this animal** — recorded here rather than as its own row, because it would otherwise be a second occurrence of this record for this species. *Discoglossus* has it from the sacral diapophysis to the urostyle, and in *Ascaphus* it cannot be separated from the coccygeoiliacus. In its place *Xenopus* has a short muscle running from the descending part of the ilium to the ventral surface of the cartilaginous epipubis, which is parked separately.

homology.notes: Epaxial identity is defined by position dorsal to the horizontal septum and by dorsal-ramus innervation, both of which hold from lampreys to mammals. The three amniote tracts are a reorganisation within that field, not new muscles. Schilling maps the character states onto a phylogeny and infers the ancestral condition at each node. Two clade-level statements from Schilling that no longer sit in occurrence rows, because he examines no bird and no crocodylian: the avian epaxial musculature is much reduced with the rigid synsacrum and shortened tail, and the three amniote tracts (transversospinal, longissimus, iliocostalis) are present across amniotes as a reorganisation of one field.
homology.teaching: The clearest case that innervation defines a muscle field: the dorsal/ventral ramus split is the same logic as the dorsal/ventral limb masses, and it is visible in a single cross-section.

muscles.name: Hypaxial musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum. Innervated by the VENTRAL rami of the spinal nerves. The abaxial part of this field is what migrates into the limb bud and becomes the appendicular musculature.

consensus.origin: Ventral surfaces of the vertebrae, the ribs, and the pelvic girdle.
consensus.insertion: Ribs, sternum, linea alba and the pelvic girdle.
consensus.action: Lateral bending in fishes; in tetrapods, trunk stabilisation, ventilation and support of the viscera against gravity.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Hypaxial myomeres
occurrences.note: Myxine glutinosa, from Schilling's Fig. 2 — a hagfish, not a lamprey. The ventral myomere parts, not yet separated from the dorsal by a horizontal septum: that septum, and with it the epaxial/hypaxial distinction, is a gnathostome character.

occurrences.name: Hypaxial myomeres
occurrences.note: Etmopterus spinax, from Schilling's Fig. 2. Ventral to the horizontal septum and still segmental; the polysegmental subvertebral and abdominal wall muscles that define the tetrapod hypaxial field are not yet present.

occurrences.name: Abdominal wall + subvertebral musculature
occurrences.note: How the hypaxial mass is apportioned tracks habitat across urodeles. Omura et al. weighed every trunk muscle in five species and found the lateral hypaxial layers taking roughly a quarter of trunk muscle mass each in the aquatic Amphiuma and Necturus against under a tenth in the terrestrial Hynobius and Ambystoma, with the rectus abdominis running the other way. The subvertebral portion rises with terrestriality alongside the epaxial mass. Proportions, not attachments — the sample is five species and three habitat classes, so it constrains what the hypaxial mass is FOR without saying where any part of it inserts.

occurrences.name: Subvertebralis, obliquus externus/internus, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis, intercostales
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) records the regional differentiation of these along the varanid trunk, which bears on how much of lateral undulation survives alongside limb-driven locomotion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus, Cieri (2018). The union of the body-wall muscles he describes individually: obliquus externus superficialis (rectus margin to the lateral dorsal ribs) and profundus (pubes to the caudal dorsal ribs), the two intercostal layers running rib to rib, the transversus (fascia deep to the sternum onto the vertebral portion of each bipartite dorsal rib), the rectus abdominis (pubis to sternum) and the levator costae (diapophysis to the next rib). **Obliquus internus is absent in varanids** — Cieri states it plainly, which is why this group has one oblique layer where a mammal has two.

occurrences.name: Abdominal wall, intercostal and subvertebral musculature
occurrences.action: Compresses the abdomen, flexes and rotates the trunk, and moves the ribs in respiration.
occurrences.innervation: Ventral primary rami of the spinal nerves throughout; the diaphragm by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). The whole ventral field, whose members have their own records and are scored there; quadratus lumborum is the subvertebral member and has none. **The diaphragm is scored as a disputed part and is the most interesting thing in this row.** It is a mammalian novelty with no counterpart in any other column here, and its nerve is the evidence for where it came from: the phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5, so the muscle is built from cervical hypaxial myotome that migrated caudally with its nerve trailing behind it. A nerve that long for a muscle that low is the record of the journey. Gest gives its origin as the xiphoid, the costal margin, the arcuate ligaments over quadratus lumborum and psoas major, and the bodies of L1-L3, all converging on a central tendon — a hypaxial sheet that ends on itself rather than on bone.

occurrences.name: Transversus and obliquus externus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Barbourula busuangensis, Prikryl et al. (2009). **A remarkable feature of this frog's trunk**: the transversus, the innermost hypaxial sheet with transversely oriented fibres, extends onto the dorsum, covers the iliolumbaris and attaches onto the dorsal fascia over the longissimus dorsi — a hypaxial muscle ending on the epaxial series, carried as `muscle: epaxial-musculature`. Its posterior margin is sharp and vertical. The obliquus externus is restricted to the anteroventral flanks, leaving the posterodorsal transversus exposed.
occurrences.note: Prikryl et al. print the specific epithet as *busagensis*; the species record uses *busuangensis*.

occurrences.name: Hypaxial muscles

parts.name: Rectus abdominis (incipient)
parts.note: Longitudinal midventral fibres, not yet separable from the hypaxial myomeres.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Caudata (generalised), Prikryl et al. (2009). In the presacral trunk the body wall is three layers — obliquus externus, obliquus internus and the innermost transversus. The longitudinally oriented fibres along the midventral line form an **incipient rectus abdominis, not yet well differentiated from the rest of the hypaxial myomeres**. Compare *Barbourula*, where the transversus has climbed onto the dorsum, and the two pipids, where the rectus abdominis has become distinct enough to reach the femur.

homology.notes: Ventral-ramus innervation is the constant. The important connection for this dataset is developmental: the abaxial portion of the hypaxial field is the source of the appendicular musculature, so the limb muscles are hypaxial derivatives that migrated out. That is why the limb's ventral (flexor) mass keeps ventral-division nerves. Schilling's mammalian synthesis, which was previously an occurrence row on a species he does not examine: the ventrovertebral musculature is strengthened by the psoas major, and the mammalian series comprises quadratus lumborum, psoas minor, the obliqui, transversus abdominis, rectus abdominis and the intercostals.
homology.teaching: Answers the question students ask once they meet the dorsal/ventral limb masses: where did those masses come from? They are the hypaxial field, migrated.

muscles.name: Caudal musculature
muscles.developmental: Somitic; the post-sacral continuation of the epaxial and hypaxial series.

consensus.origin: Caudal vertebrae — their centra, neural spines, transverse processes and haemal arches.
consensus.insertion: Successive caudal vertebrae; the caudofemoralis leaves the series to insert on the femur.
consensus.action: Tail movement; in taxa with a large tail, also counterbalance and — through the caudofemoralis — femoral retraction.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal and ventral rami of the caudal spinal nerves.

occurrences.note: Lost with the tail; the urostyle replaces the caudal series.

occurrences.name: Caudal musculature (ilio-, ischio- and caudofemoralis series)
occurrences.note: Tomańska et al. (2024) describe the Komodo dragon tail as a substantial locomotor and defensive organ, with caudal muscle mass contributing counterbalance during bipedal rearing.
occurrences.divisionNote: No division recorded, and the name will not settle it: 'ilio-, ischio- and caudofemoralis series' expands two ways — iliocaudalis/ischiocaudalis or iliofemoralis/ischiofemoralis — and both are live readings. Needs the source rather than a guess.

occurrences.note: Galictis cuja: present and scored. Ercoli et al. describe the sacrocaudalis series in full in an animal with a long, well-muscled tail — the sacrocaudalis dorsalis lateralis alone is 6.81% of hind limb muscle mass. Retained in taxa with a muscular tail and reduced in others, but that is the clade-level pattern; it had been written onto this species row as `present: "variable"` while the row carried four scored attachment rows.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The sacrocaudalis series, dorsal and ventral, medial and lateral. The dorsalis medialis is the caudal continuation of the transversospinalis: its most cranial bundle arises from the caudal and dorsal spinous process of the last lumbar vertebra, subsequent bundles from the sacral and caudal spinous processes, inserting on the cranial ends of the anterior articular processes of caudal vertebrae. Each bundle spans about three vertebrae.
occurrences.name: Sacrocaudalis dorsalis and ventralis, medialis and lateralis

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). No caudal muscles are listed, and a human coccyx has essentially none of its own. **The musculature did not vanish, it changed job**: the iliococcygeus and coccygeus of the human pelvic floor are the iliocaudalis and ischiocaudalis of a tailed tetrapod, and they are scored on those records in `muscles-hindlimb.json`. A muscle group that moved a tail now holds the pelvic viscera in place.

occurrences.name: Levatores and depressores of the tail
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. levator coccygis.** Anteriorly the origin is entirely tendinous from the dorsal surface of the sacrum, beginning anteriorly at the level of a line between the two antitrochanters. The middle bundle goes to the same position on the fourth vertebra, and the lateral fasciculus, with its tendon some- times nearly twice the size of the two former ones, goes to the fifth free vertebra, just anterior to the *Insertion.* The three fingers of the belly have separate insertions. The most proximal of these inserts fleshily and tendinously on the neural spine of the fourth free vertebra just beneath the insertion of M. ley. coccygis. The second finger goes to the same position on the fifth free vertebra, and the most distal and deepest of these three fasciculi sends a tendon to the antero-lateral corner of the pygostyle (fig. 23). The un- divided and main part of the belly continues distad to fan out over the ventro-lateral surfaces of the major upper-coverts and the dorsal surfaces of the five more medial rectrices; in figure 23 the **M. lateralis caudae.** The lateral belly arises as fleshy fibers from the aponeurosis between the caudal vertebrae and the medio-posterior edge of the ilium (fig. 23). The origin does not extend anteriorly as far as the ilium, but it does in part overlie the tendinous and fleshy origin of the medial belly which comes from the postero-medial edge of the ilium and from the above-mentioned aponeurosis. This medial part also takes fleshy origin from the transverse processes of the last fused vertebrae and the first three unfused caudal vertebrae. Two small tendons are sent to the proximo-lateral surface of the neural spine of the pygostyle (fig. 23). **M. depressor caudae.** Most of the posterior edge of the ilium, the dorso-posterior edge of the ischium, the ischio-pubic aponeurosis, the pubis posterior to the end of the ischium, and the lateral two-thirds of the interpubic liga- ment furnish fleshy origin. However, there is also fleshy attachment to the ven- tral side of the aponeurosis (fig. 24) extending from the posterior extent of the ilium ventro-posteriorly to the ischio-pubic ligaments. There is a variable number of small, deep tendons which insert on the lateral face of the pygostyle distal and dorsal to the articular area. There is strong, fleshy connection to the ventro- proximal part of the pygostyle, proximal and ventral to the articulation and the haemal foramen. There is a variable number of small, deep tendons which insert on the lateral face of the pygostyle distal and dorsal to the articular area. Superficially the major insertion is fleshy on the ventral surfaces of all the under-coverts, except the most lateral; this connection to the bases of the under-coverts is deep and proximal to the insertion of M. depress. coccygis on these feathers.

homology.notes: The caudal series is the post-sacral continuation of the trunk musculature. Its interest for this dataset is the caudofemoralis, which leaves the axial series to reach the femur and so becomes an abaxial, appendicular muscle — the one muscle that crosses the boundary this file is organised around. Schilling on the avian tail, moved here from an occurrence row: the caudal musculature is reduced to the pygostyle and its rectricial muscles. He examines no bird, so this is his synthesis rather than an observation.
homology.teaching: Pair with the caudofemoralis and the fourth trochanter: the tail powers the hindlimb in most tetrapods, and both bird and mammal locomotion required breaking that link.

muscles.name: Longissimus dorsi
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.origin: Transverse processes and the ilium, spanning many segments.
consensus.insertion: Transverse processes and ribs of more cranial vertebrae; the skull in some taxa.
consensus.action: Lateral bending and, in mammals, sagittal extension; trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. longissimus dorsi
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) refers the detailed attachment tendons of longissimus, transversospinalis and iliocostalis to Gasc (1981), Ritter (1995) and Tsuihiji (2007) rather than redescribing them.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus. Left unscored on the source's own instruction: Cieri (2018) writes that the anatomy of the epaxial muscles — longissimus dorsi, transversospinalis and iliocostalis — 'including details of insertion and origin tendons, have been described in detail previously (Gasc, 1981; Ritter, 1995; Tsuihiji, 2007) and will not be described here.' **This is a pointer, not a gap**: those three papers are what would close the lepidosaur epaxial column, and none of them is in the corpus. Cieri's contribution to the epaxial series is the supracostalis dorsus brevis, which is scored.

occurrences.name: M. longissimus thoracis et lumborum
occurrences.note: Canis familiaris. Schilling's Fig. 3 records epaxial activity in the m. longissimus thoracis et lumborum at the 6th lumbar vertebra of a dog, against Ambystoma and Dipsosaurus — the comparison that shows the mammalian tract firing for sagittal stabilisation where the sprawling tetrapods' fires for lateral bending.

occurrences.name: Longissimus
occurrences.action: Extends and laterally bends the vertebral column; the capitis part extends the head.
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C1-S1.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Transverse process to transverse process, several levels up, and by the capitis division onto the mastoid process. The intermediate tract of the erector spinae, and the one that reaches furthest forward. The mastoid end was scored as `occiput` until 2026-08-20 because the skeleton carried no mastoid element; it does now, and the row was corrected rather than left approximating a petrosal attachment onto the occipital bone.

homology.notes: One of the three longitudinal epaxial tracts of amniotes. The aponeurosis dividing it from the iliocostalis is itself a muscle attachment site in varanids — it carries the supracostalis dorsus brevis.

muscles.name: Iliocostalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.insertion: Ribs and transverse processes of more cranial vertebrae.
consensus.action: Lateral bending; rib and trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. iliocostalis
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) describes it as very thin in Varanus exanthematicus.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus. Left unscored on the source's own instruction: Cieri (2018) writes that the anatomy of the epaxial muscles — longissimus dorsi, transversospinalis and iliocostalis — 'including details of insertion and origin tendons, have been described in detail previously (Gasc, 1981; Ritter, 1995; Tsuihiji, 2007) and will not be described here.' **This is a pointer, not a gap**: those three papers are what would close the lepidosaur epaxial column, and none of them is in the corpus. Cieri's contribution to the epaxial series is the supracostalis dorsus brevis, which is scored.

occurrences.name: Iliocostalis lumborum
occurrences.attachmentNote: Galictis cuja, lumbar sector. The lateralmost lumbar epaxial muscle, robust and cylindrical, and the heaviest muscle in the paper's mass table at 10.06% of total hind limb muscle mass — 'heavy iliocostalis' is one of Ercoli et al.'s headline functional characters, tied to a mobile axial skeleton and bounding gait. NOTE THE DIRECTION: the pelvic end is the origin and the ribs are the insertion. It arises mostly fleshy from the medial surface of the ala ossis ilii and the iliac crest, tendinously from the medial aspect of the lumbodorsal fascia, and partly from the body of the last lumbar vertebra just caudal to its transverse processes. It inserts by a tendinous sheet on the caudal edge of the last two ribs at their angle and dorsal regions, on the lateral and caudal body of the last thoracic vertebra, on the dorsal surfaces of the transverse processes of the last lumbar vertebra, and elsewhere only at the base and posterolateral ends of the transverse processes and the ventral region of the accessory processes. Vertebral subsites are carried in prose rather than as landmarks, following the transversospinalis row, because skeleton.json resolves no transverse, mammillary or accessory process. This row was previously left unscored on the grounds that a table interrupted the description in the PDF text layer; both attachments read cleanly out of a `pdftotext -layout` extraction once the column offset is accounted for.

occurrences.name: Iliocostalis
occurrences.action: Extends and laterally bends the trunk and neck.
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C4-S5.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Iliac crest and sacrum to the angles of the ribs — the lateral tract of the erector spinae, and the only one of the three that ends on ribs rather than on vertebrae. In a lizard the equivalent runs the length of the trunk without the lumbar interruption an upright posture imposes.

occurrences.name: Ilio-costalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. ilio-costalis.** tThe anterior slip shows its segmental nature in its origin. Superficially there is completely tendinous origin from the surface of the anterior tendons of the posterior parts, but the transverse processes of the first three thoracic vertebrae provide tendinous and fleshy origin on the deep side. In each instance the origin is from the dorso-lateral surface of the tip of the transverse process and extends ventro-laterally on fascia nearly to the tubercle of the respective rib. 114 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE The superficial, posterior part has its origin on a calcified tendon which forms part of the origin of M. spinalis thoracis. Posteriorly the anterior ed *Insertion.* The anterior bundle of M. ilio-costalis attaches fleshily and tendinously in three places—the posterior edge of rib 1, beneath the middle of the belly of M. lev. costarum; the posterior border of the greatly inflated transverse processes of vertebrae 17 and 16 (these insertions mingle inseparably with the fibers of Mm. intertransversarii); and apo- neurotic and fascial on the most antero-ventral corner of the transverse process of vertebra 16. The superficial, posterior part forms a calcified tendon along its ventral edge; the tendon passes forward to insert on the postero-dorsal corner of the tip of the transverse process of thoracic vertebra number 3. A series of insertions are presen

homology.notes: The most lateral of the three epaxial tracts.

muscles.name: Transversospinalis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.insertion: Neural spines of more cranial vertebrae.
consensus.action: Extension and rotation of the vertebral column; segmental stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. transversospinalis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus. Left unscored on the source's own instruction: Cieri (2018) writes that the anatomy of the epaxial muscles — longissimus dorsi, transversospinalis and iliocostalis — 'including details of insertion and origin tendons, have been described in detail previously (Gasc, 1981; Ritter, 1995; Tsuihiji, 2007) and will not be described here.' **This is a pointer, not a gap**: those three papers are what would close the lepidosaur epaxial column, and none of them is in the corpus. Cieri's contribution to the epaxial series is the supracostalis dorsus brevis, which is scored.

occurrences.name: Transversospinal system (multifidus, semispinalis and relatives)
occurrences.note: Subdivided into several entities in mammals; Schilling (2011) ties that subdivision to the evolution of a mobile, rib-free lumbar region.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lumbar sector only. The medialmost epaxial series, metameres largely fused with each other and with the thoracic continuation, from the lateral spinous processes and dorsal articular processes of all lumbar vertebrae but the last, plus the lumbodorsal fascia, onto the mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae and, for the last bundle, the intermediate sacral crest of S1-2. It is continuous caudally with the sacrocaudalis dorsalis medialis, which is why the tail and the back are one series and not two.

occurrences.name: Transversospinal system
occurrences.action: Extends and rotates the vertebral column; semispinalis capitis extends the head.
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C1-L5.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The deep layer, and the one whose subdivisions are defined by how far they reach.** Gest separates them exactly that way: rotatores span one or two vertebrae, multifidus two to four, semispinalis four to six, all running from a transverse process up and medially to a spinous process. Interspinales and intertransversarii are the shortest members, joining adjacent processes of the same kind. A single fibre orientation repeated at five different lengths, given five names.

**Interspinales** (Gest). Spine to the spine above, one segment at a time, the whole length of the column. Gest calls them small and mechanically unimportant, and they are; as a homology statement they are the least modified thing in the human back, a segmental muscle still spanning one segment.

**Intertransversarii** (Gest). Transverse process to the transverse process above. Gest gives the whole series dorsal rami, which is why it is scored on an epaxial record; the cervical and lumbar members take ventral rami at least in part on most other accounts, and if that is right then some of this muscle is hypaxial and the row lumps two fields. Nothing in this source separates them.

**Multifidus** (Gest). Sacrum and the transverse processes of C3 to L5, up two to four segments onto the spines.

**Rotatores** (Gest). Transverse process to the spine one or two segments above; the shortest fascicles of the series, and the deepest.

**Semispinalis** (Gest). Transverse processes of C7-T12 to the spines four to six segments above, and, in the capitis part, onto the occipital bone between the nuchal lines. Semispinalis capitis is the only member of this series that ends on the skull, and it is most of the muscle mass behind the neck.

**Spinalis** (Gest). Spines below to spines above, and to the base of the skull. Gest counts it as the medial of the three erector spinae columns and this record is the medial epaxial tract, so it is scored here rather than beside the iliocostalis and longissimus rows — which is how the human row on `epaxial-musculature` already lists it. It runs spine-to-spine, not transverse-process-to-spine, so the record's name misdescribes this member of it.

homology.notes: The medial epaxial tract, and the one that elaborates most in mammals.

muscles.name: Supracostalis dorsus brevis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome dorsal to the horizontal septum, on the dorsal rami.

consensus.origin: The aponeurosis dividing the longissimus from the iliocostalis.
consensus.insertion: Dorsal aspect of each dorsal rib, one- to two-thirds of the way down its length.
consensus.action: Lifts each rib independently of its neighbours. Cieri (2018) positions it to produce caliper motion of the ribs — rotation about a dorsoventral axis.
consensus.innervation: Dorsal rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. supracostalis dorsus brevis
occurrences.note: Segmentally divided into triangular sheets; strongly developed in Varanus exanthematicus. Its insertion tendons are continuous with those of the obliquus externus superficialis.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed among the 16 muscles of the back region. A short dorsal rib muscle described for lepidosaurs; the human muscle nearest its position is the levatores costarum, which is scored on its own record and shares this one's dorsal-ramus supply.

homology.notes: One of two muscles Cieri (2018) finds in Varanus exanthematicus and NOT in Iguana iguana, the other being the levator costae. Both take origin from the vertebral column or its fascia rather than from adjacent ribs, so each rib can be moved independently — a different mechanical arrangement from the rib-to-rib intercostal series.
homology.openQuestion: Whether these two muscles are varanid novelties or more widely distributed among squamates is open; Cieri notes that basic body-wall muscle descriptions are lacking for most reptiles.
homology.teaching: A concrete case where adding a muscle changes what the skeleton can do: rib-to-vertebra muscles allow independent rib motion that rib-to-rib muscles cannot.

muscles.name: Levator costae
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.insertion: Fanning out onto the proximal part of the articulating rib.
consensus.action: Elevates each rib relative to its own vertebra.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. levator costae
occurrences.note: Varanus exanthematicus. A small muscle deep to the longissimus dorsi and the external intercostal, connecting each rib to its articulating vertebra. Fibres arise from the dorsocaudal aspect of the diapophysis and fan out onto the dorsal edge of the cranial aspect of the next vertebral rib segment. With the supracostalis dorsus brevis it is one of two muscles Cieri reports in Varanus and not in Iguana; because their origins are on the vertebrae rather than on other ribs, they can move each rib independently of the rib cage.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus, Cieri (2018). **This row previously stood on Iguana iguana, the one lepidosaur Cieri names as LACKING the muscle**, while its own note said 'Absent in Iguana iguana' — the row asserted presence and absence at once. Re-attributed to the animal Cieri dissected. No Iguana row replaces it: Cieri did not examine Iguana, he compares with Carrier's (1989, 1990) published account, so an absence row here would credit him with an observation he did not make.

occurrences.name: Levatores costarum
occurrences.innervation: Dorsal primary rami of spinal nerves C7-T11.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Transverse processes of C7-T11 to the rib below, medial to its angle. **Dorsal rami, and that is the point**: this is a rib muscle that belongs to the epaxial field by nerve, which is what separates it from the intercostals lying just lateral to it on ventral rami. Gest's own table draws the line in the innervation column.

occurrences.name: Levator costarum
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. levator costarum.** In each instance an individual slip arises, largely fleshily but with some tendinous fibers intermixed, from the most ventro-lateral part of the diapophysis of a thoracic vertebra. Insertion.—The fibers go ventro-posteriorly at a 45-degree angle with the vertebral column and attach to the base of the corresponding rib. The most extensive area of insertion is the anterior edge of the base of each MUSCLES OF THE VERTEBRAL COLUMN Li

homology.notes: The hypaxial counterpart of the supracostalis dorsus brevis, and the second of the two muscles Cieri finds in Varanus but not Iguana. Note the pair straddles the horizontal septum: one epaxial on dorsal rami, one hypaxial on ventral rami, doing mechanically similar jobs. Cieri (2018) reports the muscle in Varanus exanthematicus and states it is not found in Iguana iguana, on comparison with Carrier's published work rather than his own dissection of that animal. Whether it is a varanid novelty or more widespread in Lepidosauria is open — no other lepidosaur in this dataset is scored for it.
homology.teaching: Two muscles with the same mechanical role on opposite sides of the epaxial/hypaxial boundary — a reminder that the division is developmental and neural, not functional.

muscles.name: Obliquus externus
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Margin between the rectus abdominis lateralis and ventralis.
consensus.insertion: Lateral aspect of the dorsal ribs, about a third of the way down, by short tendons.
consensus.action: Compresses the body wall; contributes to ventilation and trunk stabilisation.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. obliquus externus (superficialis + profundus)
occurrences.note: Well developed in Varanus exanthematicus. The superficialis covers the lateral body wall; its insertion tendons are continuous with those of the supracostalis dorsus brevis, so the epaxial and hypaxial sheets meet at the rib.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus, Cieri (2018). Two portions. The superficialis covers the lateral body wall, arising at the margin between rectus abdominis lateralis and ventralis and inserting on the lateral aspect of the dorsal ribs about a third of the way down, by short tendons continuous with those of the supracostalis dorsus brevis. **The profundus origin on the pubes was missing from this row**: it runs cranially and craniodorsally from the pelvic girdle to the caudal aspects of the 11th and following dorsal ribs, which is what makes this muscle a pelvis-to-rib-cage connection and not only a body-wall sheet.

occurrences.name: Obliquus externus
occurrences.action: Resists long-axis torsion generated by limb support during walking; bends the body during swimming.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Fibres run dorsoanterior to ventroposterior at about 50 degrees to the body axis. Neither end reaches bone — both attachments are fascial, which is why the layer leaves no osteological correlate.

parts.name: Obliquus externus superficialis
parts.note: Present as a distinct layer in Amphiuma, Cynops and Ambystoma; absent as such in Necturus and Hynobius, where the external oblique is undivided.

occurrences.divisionNote: Omura et al. dissected five urodeles of three habitat types and found the external oblique undivided in Necturus maculosus and Hynobius nigrescens but split into a superficialis and a profundus in Amphiuma tridactylum, Cynops pyrrhogaster and Ambystoma tigrinum. The whole lateral hypaxial stack likewise runs to two, three or four layers depending on species. The split does not track habitat — one aquatic and one terrestrial species share the undivided condition — so it is polymorphic within Caudata rather than a functional grade, and scoring the clade from any one exemplar would manufacture a transition.
occurrences.note: Fibre angle is measured, not estimated: roughly 50 degrees to the body axis against roughly 145 degrees for the internal oblique, so the two layers cross at close to a right angle.
occurrences.insertion: A midline aponeurosis crossing deep to the rectus abdominis.

occurrences.name: External abdominal oblique
occurrences.action: Compresses the abdomen; flexes and rotates the trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower eight ribs to the linea alba, pubic crest and tubercle, and the anterior half of the iliac crest, fibres running downward and forward. The outermost of the three sheets, and unchanged in principle from the arrangement in any tetrapod: three layers at three angles, all on ventral rami.

homology.notes: Outermost of the four body-wall layers Cieri (2018) recognises: obliquus externus, intercostales externi, intercostales interni, transversus, from superficial to deep.

muscles.name: Intercostales externi
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.insertion: Caudal aspect of the next most cranial rib.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Mm. intercostales externi
occurrences.note: Fibres course dorsocranially at about 15° above the long axis of the body, covering the costal cartilages of the floating ribs and the dorsal third of the sternal portion of each true rib.

occurrences.name: External intercostal
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower border of a rib to the upper border of the rib below, fibres running downward and forward — the same direction as the external oblique, which is the continuation of this sheet into the abdomen. One layer, two names, divided by where the ribs stop.

homology.notes: Rib-to-rib, unlike the levator costae and supracostalis dorsus brevis, which run rib-to-vertebra. Cieri's fibre-angle measurements (about 15° here against about 60° for the interni) are what distinguish the two layers.

muscles.name: Intercostales interni
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Cranial aspect of each dorsal rib.
consensus.insertion: Sternocostal joints in the region of the true ribs; ventral aspect of each floating rib.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Mm. intercostales interni
occurrences.note: Course caudodorsally at about 60° above the long axis between the dorsal ribs, and parallel to it between the sternal segments of the true ribs.

occurrences.name: Internal, innermost and subcostal intercostals
occurrences.action: Depresses the ribs in forced expiration.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Fibres running upward and forward, opposite to the external layer. Four named muscles here are one deep sheet interrupted by the neurovascular plane: internal and innermost intercostal are the two laminae either side of it, subcostalis is the same sheet spanning two or three ribs at the back, and transversus thoracis is the same sheet again on the inner surface of the sternum. Gest lists them separately because a dissector meets them separately.

homology.notes: Third of the four body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Transversus abdominis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Medial fascia deep to the sternum, and the fascia at the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis caudal to the sternum.
consensus.insertion: Cranial aspect of the ventral quarter of the vertebral portion of each bipartite dorsal rib; the lumbodorsal fascia caudal to those ribs.
consensus.action: Compresses the abdomen; supports the viscera.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. transversus
occurrences.note: The deepest and thinnest of the body-wall muscles in Varanus exanthematicus.

occurrences.name: Transversus abdominis
occurrences.action: Resists long-axis torsion during walking, bends the body during swimming, and powers exhalation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: The deepest of the three oblique layers, with dorsoventral fibres. The only one of them reaching the vertebral column.
occurrences.origin: Transverse processes of the trunk vertebrae.
occurrences.insertion: Crosses the ventral midline to the corresponding attachment of the opposite side.

occurrences.name: Transversus abdominis
occurrences.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Lower six ribs, thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior three-quarters of the iliac crest and the inguinal ligament, to the linea alba and the pecten of the pubis, fibres running transversely. The innermost sheet; its fibres are the only ones of the three that run straight across.

occurrences.name: Transversus abdominis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. transversus abdominis.** The anterior part of the origin is by fleshy fingers which come from the deep surfaces of the last three ribs; the area of attachment is 4 or 5 centimeters dorsal to the junction of the vertebral and sternal parts of the ribs. Posteriorly this origin is aponeurotic from the ventral edge of the pubis deep to, but closely connected with, the origin of M. obliq. abdom. int. However, in the most posterior 5 centimeters of the pubic length the origin is muscular. Insertion—tIn the ventral midline a raphe from the posterior end of the sternum to the interpubic ligament forms the insertion for the M. trans. abdom. of either side. Mm. intercostales externi (intercostal superf. layer) *Insertion.* tIn the ventral midline a raphe from the posterior end of the sternum to the interpubic ligament forms the insertion for the M. trans. abdom. of either side. Mm. intercostales externi (intercostal superf. layer) and Mm. intercostales interni (intercostal, deep layer) In the region of the vertebral ribs the intercostal musculature is com- posed of two layers (figs. 25 and 29). On the sternal ribs only the super- ficial layer is found (fig. 29); if the deep layer is present at all in this area it is apparently represented by a sheet of fascia closely applied to the deep side of the superficial intercostal muscles. With this exception the intercostal muscles are chara

homology.notes: Deepest of the four body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Rectus abdominis
muscles.developmental: Somitic; myotome ventral to the horizontal septum, on the ventral rami.

consensus.origin: Pubis and the ventral pelvic girdle.
consensus.insertion: Sternum, costal cartilages and the linea alba.
consensus.action: Flexes the trunk. Schilling (2011) calls it the most important sagittal flexor of the mammalian trunk.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: M. rectus abdominis (ventralis + lateralis)
occurrences.note: Cieri (2018) distinguishes a main ventral belly from a superficial rectus abdominis lateralis; the margin between them carries the origin of the obliquus externus superficialis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Varanus exanthematicus, Cieri (2018). Fibres arise from the entire cranial aspect of the pubis and insert on the ventral aspect of the sternum, blending there with the posterior part of the pectoralis. Covers the ventral and much of the lateral abdomen; the superficial rectus abdominis lateralis is carried as a part rather than a separate row.

occurrences.note: Separable as a discrete muscle only in the more terrestrial urodeles. Omura et al. could not distinguish it from the external and internal obliques in either aquatic species they dissected — Amphiuma tridactylum and Necturus maculosus — while it separated cleanly in the semi-aquatic Cynops and the terrestrial Hynobius and Ambystoma. It is also much the smallest share of trunk muscle mass in the aquatic species and the largest in the terrestrial ones, which is the load-bearing reading: a body held off the ground needs a ventral tie between the girdles, and a swimming one does not. The description below is Taricha torosa, where it is discrete.
occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.action: Prevents the trunk sagging between the girdles during walking, and draws the pelvic and pectoral girdles toward each other.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Divided into superficial and deep portions, the halves separated at the midline by the linea alba and segmented by tendinous inscriptions. The lateral fibres of the superficial portion attach to the pectoralis rather than to bone, which is why the pectoralis takes part of its own origin from those inscriptions.
occurrences.origin: Anterior border of the pubo-ischiac plate and the ypsiloid cartilage.
occurrences.insertion: Sternum and pericardium superficially; the deep portion runs on as the rectus cervicis profundus to the hyoid.

occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.action: Flexes the trunk; compresses the abdomen.
occurrences.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11 and the subcostal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Pubis and pubic symphysis to the xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5-7. **The segmentation is visible.** The tendinous intersections that make the human 'six-pack' are the remnants of the myosepta that divide this muscle into serial blocks in a fish, and the segmental nerve supply Gest lists — seven separate nerves to one muscle — is the same fact stated in the innervation column. Pyramidalis is scored as a second part: a small triangular slip in front of the rectus, often absent, ending on the linea alba.

occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. rectus abdominis.** The posterior two-fifths of the muscle are completely apo- neurotic and come from the distal 2.5 centimeters of the pubis and from the interpubic ligament. Insertion —Superficially the insertion on the posterior end of the sternal plate is aponeurotic, but fleshy fibers make up the bulk of this attach- ment. There is also some fleshy insertion on the posterior edge of the sternal part of the last rib. *Insertion.* Superficially the insertion on the posterior end of the sternal plate is aponeurotic, but fleshy fibers make up the bulk of this attach- ment. There is also some fleshy insertion on the posterior edge of the sternal part of the last rib.

occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Pipa pipa, Prikryl et al. (2009). A thin flat muscle from the ventral surface of the trunk onto the ventral surface of the thigh, diving between the cruralis and sartorius to insert on the **ventral crista of the femur**. The second pipid to run its body wall onto the femur — *Xenopus* does the same to the praepubis and the proximal third of the femur — which makes it a pipid character rather than a one-off.

occurrences.name: Rectus abdominis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Xenopus laevis, Prikryl et al. (2009). **A body-wall muscle that reaches the femur.** It comes from the ventral surface of the body and attaches posteriorly partly to the praepubis and partly to the ventral surface of the proximal third of the femur, penetrating from the surface layer between the cruralis and the sartorius — on the anterior margin of the sartorius, according to Grobbelaar (1924). The femoral attachment is the reason this row is here at all in a pelvic-and-thigh paper. The praepubis is carried as the anterior pubis, following the paper's own term — see `epipubic-cartilage-anuran` for why that is not simply merged with the epipubis. The trunk origin is not stated in terms this dataset can hold.

homology.notes: The ventral longitudinal member of the hypaxial series, outside the four transverse body-wall layers.

muscles.name: Obliquus internus
muscles.developmental: Hypaxial; lateral plate of the body wall, deep to the external oblique.

consensus.origin: Connective tissue deep to the obliquus externus.
consensus.action: Resists long-axis torsion generated by limb support; bends the body during swimming.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Obliquus internus
occurrences.note: Fibres run ventroanterior to dorsoposterior at about 145 degrees to the body axis, close to perpendicular to those of the external oblique. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Neither attachment is skeletal. The middle of the three oblique layers, thinner than the external oblique.

occurrences.name: Internal abdominal oblique
occurrences.action: Compresses the abdomen; flexes and rotates the trunk.
occurrences.innervation: Intercostal nerves 7-11, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Thoracolumbar fascia, the anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and the inguinal ligament, to the lower three or four ribs, the linea alba and the pubic crest — fibres running upward and forward, at right angles to the external oblique outside it. Gest also lists the cremaster, which is a slip of this sheet carried down onto the spermatic cord and has no counterpart in this dataset.

occurrences.name: Obliquus abdominis internus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. obliquus abdominis internus.** Aponeurotic origin comes from the ventral edge of the pubis, from the pectineal process, or just anterior to it, caudad to within 2.5 centimeters of the posterior end of the pubis. There is close intercon- nection between this aponeurosis and the one that provides origin for M. trans. abdom. Insertion.—There is fleshy connection with the postero-lateral border of the last rib. This insertion is limited ventrally by the articulation be- tween the vertebral and sternal parts of the rib, and it extends dorsad some § centimeters. *Insertion.* There is fleshy connection with the postero-lateral border of the last rib. This insertion is limited ventrally by the articulation be- tween the vertebral and sternal parts of the rib, and it extends dorsad some § centimeters.

homology.notes: The middle layer of the tetrapod body wall. The dataset previously carried the external oblique and the transversus but not the layer between them.

muscles.name: Ypsiloideus
muscles.developmental: Hypaxial; posterior continuation of the superficial rectus abdominis.

consensus.origin: Anterior edge of the medial pubis.
consensus.action: Assists the rectus abdominis in preventing the trunk from sagging.
consensus.innervation: Ventral rami of the posterior trunk spinal nerves.

occurrences.name: Ypsiloideus
occurrences.note: Appears to be the posterior continuation of the part of the superficial rectus abdominis spanning ypsiloid cartilage and pelvic girdle, and is separated from it only formally. Described here from Taricha torosa; not yet scored in other taxa in this dataset, so its absence elsewhere is unsampled rather than observed.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Both attachments are on structures with no amniote counterpart — the ypsiloid cartilage is a salamander apomorphy, which is why this muscle has no homologue outside the group.

occurrences.note: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The ypsiloideus attaches to the ypsiloid cartilage, which is an anuran and urodele structure with no amniote counterpart, so the absence follows from the skeleton rather than from anything about the muscle.

homology.notes: Tied to the ypsiloid cartilage and so restricted to salamanders. Whether it is a discrete muscle or a named part of the rectus abdominis is a matter of convention, as the paper concedes.
